full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll start off telling you a bit about what we’re doing. The project is mainly looking at engineering students, but we’ve decided to include design and technology students, within that because I think quite a bit of your course covers engineering (yes) – kind of things and also because one of the reasons we’re looking at engineering is to do with it being male dominated. I think that’s the same in design & technology as well. We’re basically looking at women who are going on placements – are you going on placement?

Subject:	Hopefully, yeah.

Interviewer:	… and getting ideas about what people expect from their placement and also why they decided to choose the subject in the first place, and their first experiences of higher education as well. What we’re planning to do, at the end of it, is to put together a guidance document that we can give to the Engineering Council to hopefully improve the situation for women. So I’ll start by asking you a few background questions to do with design & technology and things like that. So – you do design & technology don’t you?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did design & technology ‘A’ level and art er and psychology and I did ‘AS’ levels in IT and English Literature…

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, just a …

Interviewer:	Was it a comprehensive?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Not a girls’ school or anything like that?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I did – well, I did do er design work for the university – but externally, so it was like a European commission project, which they sort of approached me and asked me to get involved in it. But that was kind of – but it was only a few days working – concept generation. No apart from that.

Interviewer:	OK. What do your parents do at all, are either of them in the industry at all?

Subject:	No. Not at all. My dad’s actually – semi retired now as well, but he was in like service work so the navy and then a prison officer – and yeah, my mum was just in admin, so no, not at all.

Interviewer:	OK. So when and why then do you think that you decided to do design & technology?

Subject:	Er, I – I really, really like art, I was always really into art, so I’ve always wanted to do something that’s creative.  That’s why I chose design. And I knew that art on its own wasn’t – well it isn’t really gonna go anywhere (yeah). But I also do – I took on – like it went, from like doing graphic GCSE to doing design technology ‘A’ level and then deciding that I really liked design technology. And so, taking my creative side through that – and it just went with that really.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have any other influences like careers advice or things like that?

Subject:	Not really erm I say, it was something silly. I like met someone on holiday who did this degree but he was at Swansea and he was just talking about it and it sounded really, really good. I didn’t realise at the time it was like exactly the same as what they offered here. But I knew that that sort of field – and then from looking through prospectuses – (I came up with this?) degree.

Interviewer:	Yes, was that before you started doing your design & technology ‘A’ level or…?

Subject:	Kind of like while I was doing design and technology ‘A’ level, yes.

Interviewer:	OK and have your family been supportive of your subject?

Subject:	Yeah, they’ve backed me – really supportive, yeah…

Interviewer:	Did you do much career research?

Subject:	Erm, not a great deal. No if I’m honest. I was talking to teachers and students mainly about what sort of course was available and – design technology it’s one of those sort of fields that – it’s not – publicised hugely what is available in like – so even when I’m looking for a placement now and you’re not quite sure how companies take it on through like into their areas – ‘cos you can go into things like research & development. Some people class that as design & technology. They like people to have a good basis – understanding (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK – did you ever consider doing any other subjects at university?

Subject:	No, I think I just had my heart set on the course and I talked – decided that I liked [this university] and it was like my first interview and they sort of accepted me there and then. So it was kind of like oh, I’ve got my first choice. So I did go to all the others and looked at different courses and different things but it was (?)

Interviewer:	What do you think it was about [this university] that appealed to you? Was it mainly the course or…?

Subject:	Erm, yeah mainly – it was the best for my course, so that’s why. It was a choice between here, [university 1], [university 2] and – well [university 2] was a bit concretey and [university 1] was in the middle of nowhere so it was OK for that. And I do like the – I like on campus – I like the community environment, so that was ideal was [this university], personally.

Interviewer:	Did you realise when you decided to do design & technology that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, I did know because it is in ‘A’ level. There was loads more lads than there is girls. It’s more – because you’ve got that whole making things thing and boys tend to be into that a lot more, so yeah, I guessed it would be.

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you at all?

Subject:	Not really. I’m quite tomboyish I suppose, so it was just like way hey, sounds like a laugh.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

Subject:	Yeah – definitely, definitely.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that more women don’t – do you think it because they don’t really know what it involves?

Subject:	I don’t know actually because well – I don’t know. I don’t know – but isn’t it - I suppose it’s something to do with they’re more communicators in like English – stuff like psychology based subjects. Don’t girls brains work in those sort of subjects, and then boys are more physical. So probably just the sciencey – I reckon that’s probably why girls aren’t into as much.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s just people’s perceptions or do you think that it really is like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I think there is actually – experiments have shown that girls – something to do with the way girls are brought up isn’t it? I don’t know. Because through psychology, we did a lot to do with girls, kind of the way you get brought up. You get brought up to sort of chat a lot and I don’t know. Talk to people and make friends better – boys are go and play with this and go and make that and do this. So…

Interviewer:	Probably at a very early age.

Subject:	Yes, I think if you want to do it you kind of know what you want to do.

Interviewer:	What do you think then would need to be done to encourage more women to move into design and technology?

Subject:	Er, I don’t know really. I think – there isn’t – design & technology you don’t – it isn’t like – it doesn’t come across as a core subject, in the same way that English, maths and science do – it comes across as very vocational and so I think when a lot of people look at it they think oh doss subjects, rather than you can go into say electronicsy bits and it’s not thought of in that way really. And I’d never have thought that I’d take design & technology on to university. It’s sort of not one of those subjects that you automatically assume

Interviewer:	Like it’s not so academic?

Subject:	Yeah, so I think it would put a lot of people off because unless you want to do something definite in design, or in engineering, then you’ve got to be careful because – like if you took a finance business degree, you could go into lots of things and I suppose you still can but people’s perceptions of say finance, or law, or English – they think oh, academic. Good grounding for anything. Whereas if you say design & technology they go – oh, doss subject – I don’t know. You have to explain it to people – a lot more than you would anything else.

Interviewer:	Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	Oh I don’t know. Problem solving – what do you mean like that?

Interviewer:	Yeah

Subject:	I think if you’re observant then you see – you spot what like erm opportunities for problems and areas that you can apply your designs to. So if you’re observant. And then, if you’ve got the ability to solve them I think that’s the – and then I suppose why – if you’re like – the opposite to closed minded – open minded – yeah – you think, I suppose you can consider everybody, because you’ve got to look at everybody from different backgrounds – so if you – yeah it’s better than – if you’re blinkered with what you think your life’s about, then you’re only going to be designing for you rather than everyone. So I think if you’ve got good bodily experiences I suppose – If you’ve done a lot you’ve got much more – a better idea.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any of those characteristics are more male – do you think they are?

Subject:	Not really. I suppose (you could have either sex?), but …

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s important that more women are encouraged into the industry, ‘cos it is bringing that kind of different perspective?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. That whole sort of thing really – I mean we’ve often sat in cars and the car seat flicked back and everyone goes God only a man could design that. But like loads of people say that sort of thing – and I don’t think, in all honesty, that a man can really design for a woman or a woman can design for a man, because when I did this project, with the university, it was to do with erm bladder incontinence, for women basically and they had – the team was made of 3 girls, and 3 boys. But how can the lads possibly know like how you feel, as a woman, if you have to use something like that? They can’t. It’s like – it’s made me realise that you really do need 2 perspectives. I mean they might come up with some good ideas but to put it into practice, you do need a woman’s opinion. I mean some of the things they come out with look like things off Star Wars or – I wouldn’t let that near me – it looks spiky and spiky and horrible. So erm, yeah, I do think you need a balance.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, disadvantages – er there’s loads of those – like people patronise you a little bit. Maybe that’s cos – maybe that’s just me, I don’t know, but yeah you do get patronised a little bit and…

Interviewer:	In what sort of way?

Subject:	I don’t know erm tutors are – not so much – well it’s kind of – it’s nice they go all out to help you, but it can feel sometimes that it’s because you’re a girl that they go all out to help you and it can be a little bit sleazy with one guy and he’s like – with the girls – he’s just really unbelievable. You think, surely you can’t get away with that. He’s very - he’ll take you from the back of the queue, bring you right in front of all these lads and help you – pretty much do it for you, which you’re not going to complain if someone’s offering to help, but the lads – then you get grief off the lads because they’re like you’re a girl. You know? And then they get – they put you at a disadvantage, if that makes sense. I think erm lads – a lot of them tend to stick together. There’s a lot of it – it’s 80% males, or something like that, on my course. So the lads being mates, or whatever, if they do group work, they stick together and it’s not very often that 3 lads come up to 1 girl and say, if there’s another lad – obviously tey don’t mind, nobody minds going like that but it just tends to be a bit like that. A bit like – you know – having one group of girls and three groups of lads. It’s weird you’d think they’d mix but they don’t really, I wouldn’t say.

Interviewer:	I was going to ask you about group work actually. Do you have to do much group work? 

Subject:	Yeah, quite a lot because it’s all about teams and stuff, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are benefits to doing group work?

Subject:	I enjoy group work because although you’ve got – you’ve got the stress of like other people relying on you – you’ve got – it’s not as stressful because I tend to put a lot more pressure on myself, if I’m doing it independently, because I know what I can do and if it’s not perfect then it annoys me and I will try and get it. I push myself, whereas when I’m in group work, you know that it’s a combination of everybody and there’s less of that pressure on your work. You don’t have as much. You get it to a good standard and when it all comes together it’s – I don’t know it’s like…

Interviewer:	Like the responsibility’s shared out?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s nice you don’t have all the problems. You can ask opinions and like discuss stuff – I prefer that and I get annoyed with myself because I can’t physically sort a problem out and it’s nice.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer working with men or women or aren’t you bothered?

Subject:	It doesn’t bother me really ‘cos it all depends on what the people are actually like. If you had an unreliable girl then I’d really rather have a guy then – ‘cos you wouldn’t mind whether they were a girl or a guy. I’d prefer working with a reliable guy.

Interviewer:	I suppose we’ve talked about this a bit already, in the project that you did but do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah – yeah, definitely. They’re always telling men to be sensitive to people’s needs so like when - I do modules where the lads might have to design things or aim towards, you know, like a 20 year old female, a 40 year old female and we did exercises like this and what do you think the aspirations of a 40 year old female would be? And what do you think they’d have in their home? And the lads were going terra cotta –a dyson hoover, things like that. And it was just – they were being told that they had to be more sensitive and to look around them a lot more, so I think yeah – they – obviously girls have other like (?) – it’s like they’re more – I don’t know softer sort of characteristics and if you mix them, I think that’s the best combination.

Interviewer:	OK, What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	The worst things have been like the amount of work. It’s all pressure driven – lets see how you cope with having so many deadlines. I mean, our course is renowned. When I first got here in freshers week, it said if you find somebody that’s not coming out their room, before you call for help, check if they’re doing an industrial design course. And it’s true – there’s so much work, but it’s good ‘cos it’s made me manage my time a lot better in general things. I juggle things and without realising it’s given me a lot more confidence.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’ll help when you do go to work as well?

Subject:	Hopefully yeah.

Interviewer:	What about the best things?

Subject:	The best things well – I don’t know. I’m sure there are some. I think – because – the best things have been because we have had so much work, they register our lectures and stuff, everyone relies so much on their lecturer for stuff that – well I’ve bonded so much more with everybody – because I see my course mates every day, all day, I’ve got a really good sound group of mates and it’s brilliant and people I live with – they don’t know anybody off their course. They know people in halls but that’s it. But they don’t know – and I tend to know everyone I live with in halls, everyone that’s on my course and it’s good because I think – I don’t know, contact wise I can go out and just go on my own and it would be great.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes. Erm well one, she was like – she wasn’t the Head, she was like a key member but she’s was brilliant, she was really, really good. She was really enthusiastic when she really knew her stuff, so - but she had to leave.

Interviewer:	Do you think that male and female lecturers teach a different type of subject or that they’ve got a different style of teaching?

Subject:	Er, yeah. She was a real feminist and er she’s very enthusiastic. So she’s – I don’t know, she kept you involved and interested in her lectures. And even the lads – a lot of them didn’t like at first and warmed to her – she was very much like erm – some people kept saying she was a dragon – she’s not, she’s just a really strong character and I mean, I don’t think she’s mad or anything, she just had her and her cats. One of those sort of women – she’s really, really good at what she does and I think she was like head hunted and taken to America to work with a university there something like that. But yeah, she’s probably good and like an inspirational person – yeah, definitely. 

Interviewer:	Do you think she was a role model?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. She came from like an arty creative side, she taught foundation art and stuff – so she was much more into like the design and relationships between a person and design – like how something made you feel. So it was – she did a lot of research in that area. It was really interesting so – maybe it was just me that connected, because it was what I was interested in, but definitely.

Interviewer:	So would you find it encouraging having more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, I think there needs to be. I mean we have – no we have a few girls like ladies – or researchers that are in the background, but there’s no main – they’re all male. I don’t think it’s a disadvantage but I do think you need, like I said earlier, the balance between male and female. Somebody that’s more approachable because if I have a problem – I mean my tutor’s great but there are some things that you prefer to talk to a female about. Maybe – I think you do need that.

Interviewer:	OK, what aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had, do you think will help you when you go on your placement?

Subject:	We’ve had a lot of advice.

Interviewer:	And do you think you’ll use all the skills that you’ve learnt?

Subject:	Hopefully, I mean there’s things I don’t think I’ll use like I don’t think I’ll actually go into a design concept generation job I – well, I was talking to my er – well it’s the person who does the careers area, and he was saying that a lot of companies like people to go into their development work because as you develop other people’s idea – it’s like people that did – automotive – the top designers in the country – that the automotive designs they bring over from Japan and they probably do that. They bring on like the best in the country and you work on developing theirs – some of their ideas, and you throw your ideas, from the sidelines like back in and they like that so …

Interviewer:	It sounds very interesting.

Subject:	Yeah, so that I think’s great, because you do – and you do have to have a good basic understanding, like erm the engineering drawing – like I can understand engineering drawings from that field and I’ve got ideas, about research between sexes and ethnic backgrounds and stuff that’s design related and at the same time I understand manufacturing processes so you can work on things – casting things – you know the process and I think that’s really important that you can do everything and maybe multi-functional…

Interviewer:	Did you realise that the course did include so much engineering based stuff?

Subject:	I didn’t, at the time, realise there was so much mechanical – like electrical maths and stuff in the first year, ‘cos I did get quite stressed out there. They let me – they kept that quite quiet. Everyone now and go ha, ha, you have to do all this really hard stuff. No they did try and stress us out, they were like, you think you’re going to have a life? You’re not. And they were right. Seriously, with all this work and you thought, ah, I thought they were just trying to scare me so – but they were quite good.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that the work experience that you’ve got will help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I think – it was good to work in teams and you kind of – you got a feel for what it would be like bouncing ideas off other people. I mean I didn’t know anybody else. I was the only first year in that and I was like about 4 second years and a couple of third years – and everybody was totally at sort of different levels on the course. Again, I was so scared, because I’d never done anything like that in my work. Looking at my work was absolutely rubbish, it’s like looking at theirs was – they were like, don’t worry, don’t worry. They were so much further on but it was nice to see how they took my – some of my ideas from mood boards and work that came out and they developed it and they’d be oh that’s quite good and then you’d kind of work with it. So it was really good, working with people I didn’t know. And that – I don’t know it builds up your relationship skills, doesn’t it? So yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you feel really and prepared to go on placement work?

Subject:	Erm, not really. I sort of do. I feel more ready about going to placement than I do about going into my third year. I keep saying this I keep saying, oh if I don’t get a placement – what am I going to do, m I going to defer a year? Because I don’t feel like I’ve had enough time to practice everything I’ve learnt. Because they give you so much work, what you learn you don’t practice. But then I don’t think I would, if I did have the time. I’d say I did, but I wouldn’t and so, I want that year to help me grow up a little bit I suppose. Now I have some ideas about final projects and dissertations because if someone asked me now, I’d be just like I haven’t actually got a clue. I don’t want to do it. I just want to stay in my second year, it’s much better – become a first year again. But yeah,…

Interviewer:	Quite a lot of people on your course have said that. I don’t know whether it’s something like…

Subject:	Said what? They want – that they’re

Interviewer:	That they’re not ready to go into their 3rd year yet and I don’t know whether that differs from other subjects because you do this final year project.

Subject:	It’s – (?) is, (?) is a final year project, which you’ve got to be really into in a way. It’s just getting me worried. You need to have some ideas because all the design work we’re doing is like really pathetic. It’s sort of like design a hand held product. Design like – I mean we did mechanical coat hangers and little things. I mean it’s so we can get the understanding – all they want is for you to understand the mechanical approach and then put it in a really simple product, and then you’re learning. But you’ve got to think my final year project’s got to be actually something that might be taken on board by a company or would have to be good enough to gain sponsorship for. People are going to look at you in the degree show. I haven’t got a clue. I mean – I’ve never had to work on something as important as that, so yeah it’s like a mental blank.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you for going into the industry?

Subject:	Er, not really. I think to – it’s really hard again, you know looking to the industry for a placement. And I mean, they forward everyone what they’ve got. I think they could do a bit more sort of ground work on companies and try and get more people placements because – or even just like give you a list and say try these companies or but they’re never – you just get the odd forwarded email thing, looking for a placement – and everybody goes for that one and then it seems like – it’s not great. And people in past years have all said the same about the placement. At the same time, if companies aren’t coming to him then it’s a hell of a lot of to ask of him isn’t it? You know – so it’s (lost words) but I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Did people come in and talk to you, or anything like that?

Subject:	Well [company 1] – [company 1] are the only ones that actually came in and actually said. That’s cos they’re [town] based. So yeah, I think if they’re local they do try and come in and say – Oh [company 2], but then that was because that was about the day – I don’t know – that was somewhere close to here.

Interviewer:	Why do you want to go on placement then?

Subject:	Mainly because of the experience then, to give you some ideas and possibly find an opportunity for a final project.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on placement?

Subject:	No. My parents are encouraging but then that’s ‘cos they know I really, really wanted to get on one so they’re very much like. Come on you should be getting a placement – let’s look for a placement (lost words.) I will, because it scares me, the thought of sitting in front of the internet, for 5 hours, sifting, looking for engineering placements and no, that’s not really what I’m looking for. Well, get – until you’ve got something, go for that and it’s oh yeah, really good and then you look at it and it goes, we want someone that does chemistry or something like that. And you say like, no.

Interviewer:	What sorts of things have you been looking for in companies then?

Subject:	Erm, looking at sort of placements that have got product development. So things like all the packing companies – product sale companies, things like [company 3] and things that have products and then have packaging so that you can look at both – and have definite brands, because people look at sort of branding and stuff like that. [company 1] was quite interesting. I went – perhaps for like a tour round that, erm having a look at the different places they do but that was quite business related. Erm, had an interview at [company 2] – which – that again that wasn’t really – when I actually went there I thought oh, I hope I don’t get this. Ah no, because you’d be thinking God, you’d want to accept it just because it was a placement and you’d think I might not get another one but I’m glad I didn’t get it because it was very much like testing [product] and stuff and I was saying hmmm, I don’t really want to spend a year, testing [product]. And actually they were like all our [product] must be at human standards and so I was thinking – you know, and it was to do with product development of the recipes. I was thinking no. But there was – the one for [company 4] looked really good and that was to do with like graphic. You worked alongside the design team and the graphic team, so that looked really interesting.

Interviewer:	Is the main thing that you’ve looked at been the type of work that they do or have you looked at the things like the career prospects, when you’ve finished or training opportunities – anything like that?

Subject:	Not really. I should – that’s quite a good idea. I should write that – no, just looking at what they offer a lot. Like whether it’s the right sort of field, whether they do internships or placements and if they don’t I just apply anyway, and just say what I do. Say I’m interested in their products more than something – stuff like that.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the best things and the worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Er, the worst thing – just it being so daunting, when you first start, ‘cos I’m going to be like the student. Er everyone’s going to be – oh, you’re a student. But a lot of placements said oh yeah, but after a months everyone forgets you’re a student, you just become part of the workforce. That sounds quite good. And it’s just having that break from Uni I suppose. Just getting out into the real world and getting a taster you know – that’s the best thing – definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	I think sort of more responsibility in the first place. A lot of people relying on you and I won’t be able to blag it – I’m going to have to – it’ll be like I won’t know what to say – I don’t know it’s just – well it’s gonna be – I don’t know. It’s just gonna be like something I’ve never really experienced because the only work I’ve ever really done is gonna be like the little jobs in the summer, and it’s not really the same at all.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll get treated differently at work to university?

Subject:	Definitely, especially – but on a different levels. Well, hopefully – unless people do keep treating you the same but yeah, I think people – you’ll get more respect won’t you because you’re doing something and if you do it well, people are gonna respect you for that.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Haven’t a clue – probably on the dole (laughs) No, hopefully working with er possibly someone who’ll employ for the placement. I mean if not, I don’t know maybe - I thought about doing a masters. Or, if all that fails I can be a teacher.

Interviewer:	What would be like your ideal career then?

Subject:	Oh doing what that lad does, which I met on holiday – he works for Lego in Denmark, and I thought that sounds like a great job. I was like yes, that’s what I’m going to do. Design toys.

Interviewer:	Do you see yourself like going into management or …?

Subject:	To going into research and development I think – well something like that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in design & technology?

Subject:	I think it’s all about luck really because if you get the right company and the right placement, then yeah your prospects are good and you’ll get a good high paid job but if you get working for a little design consultancy where like – it all depends on a lot like economic status like of the company because if people don’t have the money to put into design then you’re not gonna get a great job. You’re not gonna – there’s not gonna be a lot, whereas if there is good economic status, people are all up for throwing money in, investing in getting designs up and I don’t know – so – I mean you could land like a brilliant job or you can do something – I don’t know do technology and science

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently…?

Subject:	I can’t think of anything else I’d want to do so I’m inclined to think well, yeah, in my eyes that kind of means I made the right decision I think. So yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, What 5 words would you use to describe like the design & technology industry?

Subject:	Oh God erm – the industry? Erm, high – quite fast moving really, stressful, erm exciting – it is really exciting because you’re at the front edge – you do see everything coming – erm, (?)

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is masculine? 

Subject:	At the moment it is, yeah but each year I think more and more girls do start going into it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will improve then?

Subject:	Yeah definitely. I mean everything - I mean you’ve got web sites on women and engineering and women designers and things that you can basically live on and stuff like that. I mean they’re trying aren’t they, to get more women into it, so…yeah, I think it should.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that it is so masculine or male dominated, will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	No not really – almost an advantage because it might – a lot of companies and stuff are – I mean if they’re looking for more women, in their companies, then you’re at an advantage that you’re doing all the stuff that the blokes do. But you’re bringing something different for them, so yeah I think it’s a good thing occasionally.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything thanks very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll start off telling you a bit about what we’re doing. The project is mainly looking at engineering students, but we’ve decided to include design and technology students, within that because I think quite a bit of your course covers engineering (yes) – kind of things and also because one of the reasons we’re looking at engineering is to do with it being male dominated. I think that’s the same in design & technology as well. We’re basically looking at women who are going on placements – are you going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: … and getting ideas about what people expect from their placement and also why they decided to choose the subject in the first place, and their first experiences of higher education as well. What we’re planning to do, at the end of it, is to put together a guidance document that we can give to the Engineering Council to hopefully improve the situation for women. So I’ll start by asking you a few background questions to do with design & technology and things like that. So – you do design & technology don’t you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What A levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did design & technology ‘A’ level and art er and psychology and I did ‘AS’ levels in IT and English Literature…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, just a …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it a comprehensive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not a girls’ school or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I did – well, I did do er design work for the university – but externally, so it was like a European commission project, which they sort of approached me and asked me to get involved in it. But that was kind of – but it was only a few days working – concept generation. No apart from that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do your parents do at all, are either of them in the industry at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Not at all. My dad’s actually – semi retired now as well, but he was in like service work so the navy and then a prison officer – and yeah, my mum was just in admin, so no, not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. So when and why then do you think that you decided to do design & technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I – I really, really like art, I was always really into art, so I’ve always wanted to do something that’s creative. That’s why I chose design. And I knew that art on its own wasn’t – well it isn’t really gonna go anywhere (yeah). But I also do – I took on – like it went, from like doing graphic GCSE to doing design technology ‘A’ level and then deciding that I really liked design technology. And so, taking my creative side through that – and it just went with that really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have any other influences like careers advice or things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really erm I say, it was something silly. I like met someone on holiday who did this degree but he was at Swansea and he was just talking about it and it sounded really, really good. I didn’t realise at the time it was like exactly the same as what they offered here. But I knew that that sort of field – and then from looking through prospectuses – (I came up with this?) degree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, was that before you started doing your design & technology ‘A’ level or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Kind of like while I was doing design and technology ‘A’ level, yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK and have your family been supportive of your subject?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they’ve backed me – really supportive, yeah…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much career research?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not a great deal. No if I’m honest. I was talking to teachers and students mainly about what sort of course was available and – design technology it’s one of those sort of fields that – it’s not – publicised hugely what is available in like – so even when I’m looking for a placement now and you’re not quite sure how companies take it on through like into their areas – ‘cos you can go into things like research & development. Some people class that as design & technology. They like people to have a good basis – understanding (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK – did you ever consider doing any other subjects at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think I just had my heart set on the course and I talked – decided that I liked [this university] and it was like my first interview and they sort of accepted me there and then. So it was kind of like oh, I’ve got my first choice. So I did go to all the others and looked at different courses and different things but it was (?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think it was about [this university] that appealed to you? Was it mainly the course or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah mainly – it was the best for my course, so that’s why. It was a choice between here, [university 1], [university 2] and – well [university 2] was a bit concretey and [university 1] was in the middle of nowhere so it was OK for that. And I do like the – I like on campus – I like the community environment, so that was ideal was [this university], personally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you realise when you decided to do design & technology that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I did know because it is in ‘A’ level. There was loads more lads than there is girls. It’s more – because you’ve got that whole making things thing and boys tend to be into that a lot more, so yeah, I guessed it would be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it ever bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I’m quite tomboyish I suppose, so it was just like way hey, sounds like a laugh.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – definitely, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that more women don’t – do you think it because they don’t really know what it involves?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know actually because well – I don’t know. I don’t know – but isn’t it - I suppose it’s something to do with they’re more communicators in like English – stuff like psychology based subjects. Don’t girls brains work in those sort of subjects, and then boys are more physical. So probably just the sciencey – I reckon that’s probably why girls aren’t into as much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s just people’s perceptions or do you think that it really is like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think there is actually – experiments have shown that girls – something to do with the way girls are brought up isn’t it? I don’t know. Because through psychology, we did a lot to do with girls, kind of the way you get brought up. You get brought up to sort of chat a lot and I don’t know. Talk to people and make friends better – boys are go and play with this and go and make that and do this. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Probably at a very early age.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think if you want to do it you kind of know what you want to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think then would need to be done to encourage more women to move into design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t know really. I think – there isn’t – design & technology you don’t – it isn’t like – it doesn’t come across as a core subject, in the same way that English, maths and science do – it comes across as very vocational and so I think when a lot of people look at it they think oh doss subjects, rather than you can go into say electronicsy bits and it’s not thought of in that way really. And I’d never have thought that I’d take design & technology on to university. It’s sort of not one of those subjects that you automatically assume

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like it’s not so academic?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, so I think it would put a lot of people off because unless you want to do something definite in design, or in engineering, then you’ve got to be careful because – like if you took a finance business degree, you could go into lots of things and I suppose you still can but people’s perceptions of say finance, or law, or English – they think oh, academic. Good grounding for anything. Whereas if you say design & technology they go – oh, doss subject – I don’t know. You have to explain it to people – a lot more than you would anything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I don’t know. Problem solving – what do you mean like that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think if you’re observant then you see – you spot what like erm opportunities for problems and areas that you can apply your designs to. So if you’re observant. And then, if you’ve got the ability to solve them I think that’s the – and then I suppose why – if you’re like – the opposite to closed minded – open minded – yeah – you think, I suppose you can consider everybody, because you’ve got to look at everybody from different backgrounds – so if you – yeah it’s better than – if you’re blinkered with what you think your life’s about, then you’re only going to be designing for you rather than everyone. So I think if you’ve got good bodily experiences I suppose – If you’ve done a lot you’ve got much more – a better idea.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any of those characteristics are more male – do you think they are?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I suppose (you could have either sex?), but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s important that more women are encouraged into the industry, ‘cos it is bringing that kind of different perspective?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. That whole sort of thing really – I mean we’ve often sat in cars and the car seat flicked back and everyone goes God only a man could design that. But like loads of people say that sort of thing – and I don’t think, in all honesty, that a man can really design for a woman or a woman can design for a man, because when I did this project, with the university, it was to do with erm bladder incontinence, for women basically and they had – the team was made of 3 girls, and 3 boys. But how can the lads possibly know like how you feel, as a woman, if you have to use something like that? They can’t. It’s like – it’s made me realise that you really do need 2 perspectives. I mean they might come up with some good ideas but to put it into practice, you do need a woman’s opinion. I mean some of the things they come out with look like things off Star Wars or – I wouldn’t let that near me – it looks spiky and spiky and horrible. So erm, yeah, I do think you need a balance.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, disadvantages – er there’s loads of those – like people patronise you a little bit. Maybe that’s cos – maybe that’s just me, I don’t know, but yeah you do get patronised a little bit and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In what sort of way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know erm tutors are – not so much – well it’s kind of – it’s nice they go all out to help you, but it can feel sometimes that it’s because you’re a girl that they go all out to help you and it can be a little bit sleazy with one guy and he’s like – with the girls – he’s just really unbelievable. You think, surely you can’t get away with that. He’s very - he’ll take you from the back of the queue, bring you right in front of all these lads and help you – pretty much do it for you, which you’re not going to complain if someone’s offering to help, but the lads – then you get grief off the lads because they’re like you’re a girl. You know? And then they get – they put you at a disadvantage, if that makes sense. I think erm lads – a lot of them tend to stick together. There’s a lot of it – it’s 80% males, or something like that, on my course. So the lads being mates, or whatever, if they do group work, they stick together and it’s not very often that 3 lads come up to 1 girl and say, if there’s another lad – obviously tey don’t mind, nobody minds going like that but it just tends to be a bit like that. A bit like – you know – having one group of girls and three groups of lads. It’s weird you’d think they’d mix but they don’t really, I wouldn’t say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I was going to ask you about group work actually. Do you have to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, quite a lot because it’s all about teams and stuff, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are benefits to doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I enjoy group work because although you’ve got – you’ve got the stress of like other people relying on you – you’ve got – it’s not as stressful because I tend to put a lot more pressure on myself, if I’m doing it independently, because I know what I can do and if it’s not perfect then it annoys me and I will try and get it. I push myself, whereas when I’m in group work, you know that it’s a combination of everybody and there’s less of that pressure on your work. You don’t have as much. You get it to a good standard and when it all comes together it’s – I don’t know it’s like…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like the responsibility’s shared out?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s nice you don’t have all the problems. You can ask opinions and like discuss stuff – I prefer that and I get annoyed with myself because I can’t physically sort a problem out and it’s nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer working with men or women or aren’t you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t bother me really ‘cos it all depends on what the people are actually like. If you had an unreliable girl then I’d really rather have a guy then – ‘cos you wouldn’t mind whether they were a girl or a guy. I’d prefer working with a reliable guy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I suppose we’ve talked about this a bit already, in the project that you did but do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – yeah, definitely. They’re always telling men to be sensitive to people’s needs so like when - I do modules where the lads might have to design things or aim towards, you know, like a 20 year old female, a 40 year old female and we did exercises like this and what do you think the aspirations of a 40 year old female would be? And what do you think they’d have in their home? And the lads were going terra cotta –a dyson hoover, things like that. And it was just – they were being told that they had to be more sensitive and to look around them a lot more, so I think yeah – they – obviously girls have other like (?) – it’s like they’re more – I don’t know softer sort of characteristics and if you mix them, I think that’s the best combination.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The worst things have been like the amount of work. It’s all pressure driven – lets see how you cope with having so many deadlines. I mean, our course is renowned. When I first got here in freshers week, it said if you find somebody that’s not coming out their room, before you call for help, check if they’re doing an industrial design course. And it’s true – there’s so much work, but it’s good ‘cos it’s made me manage my time a lot better in general things. I juggle things and without realising it’s given me a lot more confidence.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’ll help when you do go to work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the best things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best things well – I don’t know. I’m sure there are some. I think – because – the best things have been because we have had so much work, they register our lectures and stuff, everyone relies so much on their lecturer for stuff that – well I’ve bonded so much more with everybody – because I see my course mates every day, all day, I’ve got a really good sound group of mates and it’s brilliant and people I live with – they don’t know anybody off their course. They know people in halls but that’s it. But they don’t know – and I tend to know everyone I live with in halls, everyone that’s on my course and it’s good because I think – I don’t know, contact wise I can go out and just go on my own and it would be great.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Erm well one, she was like – she wasn’t the Head, she was like a key member but she’s was brilliant, she was really, really good. She was really enthusiastic when she really knew her stuff, so - but she had to leave.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that male and female lecturers teach a different type of subject or that they’ve got a different style of teaching?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah. She was a real feminist and er she’s very enthusiastic. So she’s – I don’t know, she kept you involved and interested in her lectures. And even the lads – a lot of them didn’t like at first and warmed to her – she was very much like erm – some people kept saying she was a dragon – she’s not, she’s just a really strong character and I mean, I don’t think she’s mad or anything, she just had her and her cats. One of those sort of women – she’s really, really good at what she does and I think she was like head hunted and taken to America to work with a university there something like that. But yeah, she’s probably good and like an inspirational person – yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think she was a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. She came from like an arty creative side, she taught foundation art and stuff – so she was much more into like the design and relationships between a person and design – like how something made you feel. So it was – she did a lot of research in that area. It was really interesting so – maybe it was just me that connected, because it was what I was interested in, but definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you find it encouraging having more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think there needs to be. I mean we have – no we have a few girls like ladies – or researchers that are in the background, but there’s no main – they’re all male. I don’t think it’s a disadvantage but I do think you need, like I said earlier, the balance between male and female. Somebody that’s more approachable because if I have a problem – I mean my tutor’s great but there are some things that you prefer to talk to a female about. Maybe – I think you do need that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had, do you think will help you when you go on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We’ve had a lot of advice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you think you’ll use all the skills that you’ve learnt?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, I mean there’s things I don’t think I’ll use like I don’t think I’ll actually go into a design concept generation job I – well, I was talking to my er – well it’s the person who does the careers area, and he was saying that a lot of companies like people to go into their development work because as you develop other people’s idea – it’s like people that did – automotive – the top designers in the country – that the automotive designs they bring over from Japan and they probably do that. They bring on like the best in the country and you work on developing theirs – some of their ideas, and you throw your ideas, from the sidelines like back in and they like that so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It sounds very interesting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, so that I think’s great, because you do – and you do have to have a good basic understanding, like erm the engineering drawing – like I can understand engineering drawings from that field and I’ve got ideas, about research between sexes and ethnic backgrounds and stuff that’s design related and at the same time I understand manufacturing processes so you can work on things – casting things – you know the process and I think that’s really important that you can do everything and maybe multi-functional…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you realise that the course did include so much engineering based stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t, at the time, realise there was so much mechanical – like electrical maths and stuff in the first year, ‘cos I did get quite stressed out there. They let me – they kept that quite quiet. Everyone now and go ha, ha, you have to do all this really hard stuff. No they did try and stress us out, they were like, you think you’re going to have a life? You’re not. And they were right. Seriously, with all this work and you thought, ah, I thought they were just trying to scare me so – but they were quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that the work experience that you’ve got will help you when you go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think – it was good to work in teams and you kind of – you got a feel for what it would be like bouncing ideas off other people. I mean I didn’t know anybody else. I was the only first year in that and I was like about 4 second years and a couple of third years – and everybody was totally at sort of different levels on the course. Again, I was so scared, because I’d never done anything like that in my work. Looking at my work was absolutely rubbish, it’s like looking at theirs was – they were like, don’t worry, don’t worry. They were so much further on but it was nice to see how they took my – some of my ideas from mood boards and work that came out and they developed it and they’d be oh that’s quite good and then you’d kind of work with it. So it was really good, working with people I didn’t know. And that – I don’t know it builds up your relationship skills, doesn’t it? So yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel really and prepared to go on placement work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. I sort of do. I feel more ready about going to placement than I do about going into my third year. I keep saying this I keep saying, oh if I don’t get a placement – what am I going to do, m I going to defer a year? Because I don’t feel like I’ve had enough time to practice everything I’ve learnt. Because they give you so much work, what you learn you don’t practice. But then I don’t think I would, if I did have the time. I’d say I did, but I wouldn’t and so, I want that year to help me grow up a little bit I suppose. Now I have some ideas about final projects and dissertations because if someone asked me now, I’d be just like I haven’t actually got a clue. I don’t want to do it. I just want to stay in my second year, it’s much better – become a first year again. But yeah,…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Quite a lot of people on your course have said that. I don’t know whether it’s something like…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Said what? They want – that they’re

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That they’re not ready to go into their 3rd year yet and I don’t know whether that differs from other subjects because you do this final year project.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s – (?) is, (?) is a final year project, which you’ve got to be really into in a way. It’s just getting me worried. You need to have some ideas because all the design work we’re doing is like really pathetic. It’s sort of like design a hand held product. Design like – I mean we did mechanical coat hangers and little things. I mean it’s so we can get the understanding – all they want is for you to understand the mechanical approach and then put it in a really simple product, and then you’re learning. But you’ve got to think my final year project’s got to be actually something that might be taken on board by a company or would have to be good enough to gain sponsorship for. People are going to look at you in the degree show. I haven’t got a clue. I mean – I’ve never had to work on something as important as that, so yeah it’s like a mental blank.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university could do anything more to help prepare you for going into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, not really. I think to – it’s really hard again, you know looking to the industry for a placement. And I mean, they forward everyone what they’ve got. I think they could do a bit more sort of ground work on companies and try and get more people placements because – or even just like give you a list and say try these companies or but they’re never – you just get the odd forwarded email thing, looking for a placement – and everybody goes for that one and then it seems like – it’s not great. And people in past years have all said the same about the placement. At the same time, if companies aren’t coming to him then it’s a hell of a lot of to ask of him isn’t it? You know – so it’s (lost words) but I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did people come in and talk to you, or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well [company 1] – [company 1] are the only ones that actually came in and actually said. That’s cos they’re [town] based. So yeah, I think if they’re local they do try and come in and say – Oh [company 2], but then that was because that was about the day – I don’t know – that was somewhere close to here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you want to go on placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mainly because of the experience then, to give you some ideas and possibly find an opportunity for a final project.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. My parents are encouraging but then that’s ‘cos they know I really, really wanted to get on one so they’re very much like. Come on you should be getting a placement – let’s look for a placement (lost words.) I will, because it scares me, the thought of sitting in front of the internet, for 5 hours, sifting, looking for engineering placements and no, that’s not really what I’m looking for. Well, get – until you’ve got something, go for that and it’s oh yeah, really good and then you look at it and it goes, we want someone that does chemistry or something like that. And you say like, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sorts of things have you been looking for in companies then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, looking at sort of placements that have got product development. So things like all the packing companies – product sale companies, things like [company 3] and things that have products and then have packaging so that you can look at both – and have definite brands, because people look at sort of branding and stuff like that. [company 1] was quite interesting. I went – perhaps for like a tour round that, erm having a look at the different places they do but that was quite business related. Erm, had an interview at [company 2] – which – that again that wasn’t really – when I actually went there I thought oh, I hope I don’t get this. Ah no, because you’d be thinking God, you’d want to accept it just because it was a placement and you’d think I might not get another one but I’m glad I didn’t get it because it was very much like testing [product] and stuff and I was saying hmmm, I don’t really want to spend a year, testing [product]. And actually they were like all our [product] must be at human standards and so I was thinking – you know, and it was to do with product development of the recipes. I was thinking no. But there was – the one for [company 4] looked really good and that was to do with like graphic. You worked alongside the design team and the graphic team, so that looked really interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the main thing that you’ve looked at been the type of work that they do or have you looked at the things like the career prospects, when you’ve finished or training opportunities – anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I should – that’s quite a good idea. I should write that – no, just looking at what they offer a lot. Like whether it’s the right sort of field, whether they do internships or placements and if they don’t I just apply anyway, and just say what I do. Say I’m interested in their products more than something – stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the best things and the worst things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the worst thing – just it being so daunting, when you first start, ‘cos I’m going to be like the student. Er everyone’s going to be – oh, you’re a student. But a lot of placements said oh yeah, but after a months everyone forgets you’re a student, you just become part of the workforce. That sounds quite good. And it’s just having that break from Uni I suppose. Just getting out into the real world and getting a taster you know – that’s the best thing – definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think sort of more responsibility in the first place. A lot of people relying on you and I won’t be able to blag it – I’m going to have to – it’ll be like I won’t know what to say – I don’t know it’s just – well it’s gonna be – I don’t know. It’s just gonna be like something I’ve never really experienced because the only work I’ve ever really done is gonna be like the little jobs in the summer, and it’s not really the same at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll get treated differently at work to university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, especially – but on a different levels. Well, hopefully – unless people do keep treating you the same but yeah, I think people – you’ll get more respect won’t you because you’re doing something and if you do it well, people are gonna respect you for that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Haven’t a clue – probably on the dole (laughs) No, hopefully working with er possibly someone who’ll employ for the placement. I mean if not, I don’t know maybe - I thought about doing a masters. Or, if all that fails I can be a teacher.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would be like your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh doing what that lad does, which I met on holiday – he works for Lego in Denmark, and I thought that sounds like a great job. I was like yes, that’s what I’m going to do. Design toys.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you see yourself like going into management or …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To going into research and development I think – well something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in design & technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s all about luck really because if you get the right company and the right placement, then yeah your prospects are good and you’ll get a good high paid job but if you get working for a little design consultancy where like – it all depends on a lot like economic status like of the company because if people don’t have the money to put into design then you’re not gonna get a great job. You’re not gonna – there’s not gonna be a lot, whereas if there is good economic status, people are all up for throwing money in, investing in getting designs up and I don’t know – so – I mean you could land like a brilliant job or you can do something – I don’t know do technology and science

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can’t think of anything else I’d want to do so I’m inclined to think well, yeah, in my eyes that kind of means I made the right decision I think. So yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What 5 words would you use to describe like the design & technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God erm – the industry? Erm, high – quite fast moving really, stressful, erm exciting – it is really exciting because you’re at the front edge – you do see everything coming – erm, (?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment it is, yeah but each year I think more and more girls do start going into it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will improve then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah definitely. I mean everything - I mean you’ve got web sites on women and engineering and women designers and things that you can basically live on and stuff like that. I mean they’re trying aren’t they, to get more women into it, so…yeah, I think it should.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that it is so masculine or male dominated, will cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No not really – almost an advantage because it might – a lot of companies and stuff are – I mean if they’re looking for more women, in their companies, then you’re at an advantage that you’re doing all the stuff that the blokes do. But you’re bringing something different for them, so yeah I think it’s a good thing occasionally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything thanks very much.
